title: Septic arthritis of a native joint (adult)
subject: surgery-trauma
setting: Emergency department, orthopaedic and rheumatology wards
summary: Treat an acute hot swollen joint as septic until proven otherwise: aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals and take blood cultures before antibiotics, start empirical IV antibiotics chosen by risk group, and drain the joint by repeated aspiration or arthroscopic or open washout.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Acute monoarthritis with pain, warmth, effusion and restricted movement; the knee is most often affected, then hip, shoulder, ankle and wrist. Fever is often absent.
Risk factors: age over 80, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, prosthetic joint, recent joint surgery or injection, skin infection or ulcers, injecting drug use, and immunosuppression.

Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause, then streptococci. Gram-negative organisms are more likely in older, frail or immunocompromised patients and injecting drug users. Consider gonococcal infection in sexually active young adults (migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, skin pustules).
Crystals in the fluid do not exclude infection; gout and sepsis can coexist.
In India, also consider tuberculous arthritis (subacute or chronic course) and, in people with diabetes from endemic areas, melioidosis.

sections.title: Before antibiotics
items: Aspirate the joint before starting antibiotics (image-guided for the hip) and send fluid for Gram stain, culture (also inoculate blood culture bottles), cell count and polarised microscopy for crystals.
Take blood cultures before antibiotics in every patient.
Septic or unstable patient: start the sepsis bundle and give antibiotics straight after blood cultures; do not delay antibiotics for aspiration.
Suspected prosthetic joint infection: refer urgently to orthopaedics and do not aspirate in the ED.
Do not inject corticosteroid into an undiagnosed hot joint.

sections.title: Investigations
items: FBC, CRP, ESR, creatinine, liver function and glucose; normal inflammatory markers do not exclude infection.
Synovial fluid: a very high white cell count with neutrophil predominance supports infection, but a negative Gram stain or lower count does not exclude it.
Plain X-ray as a baseline (and to look for osteomyelitis or chondrocalcinosis); ultrasound to confirm hip effusion or guide aspiration; MRI if adjacent osteomyelitis is suspected.
Suspected gonococcal infection: nucleic acid amplification tests from urethra or cervix, rectum and pharynx.

sections.title: Empirical antibiotics (BSR 2006, adapt to local antibiogram)
items: No risk factors for atypical organisms: flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 6 hours. Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours is an alternative for MSSA cover.
Penicillin allergy: clindamycin 450 to 600 mg IV every 6 hours, or a 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin if the allergy is not severe.
High risk of gram-negative infection (older, frail, recurrent urinary infection, recent abdominal surgery): cefuroxime 1.5 g IV every 8 hours or another 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin.
MRSA risk (known carriage, recent healthcare exposure, or high local prevalence as in many Indian hospitals): vancomycin plus a 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin.
Suspected gonococcal arthritis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily.

Duration: conventionally IV for up to 2 weeks or until improving, then oral to complete about 6 weeks in total (BSR 2006). Shorter courses after adequate surgical drainage are increasingly used on specialist advice.

sections.title: Joint drainage
items: Drain every septic joint: repeated needle aspiration to dryness, or arthroscopic or open washout. Involve orthopaedics early; the hip usually needs surgical drainage.
Septic, unwell patient: emergent surgical drainage as soon as it is safe, within 6 hours (BOAST principles), because cartilage damage is time-critical.
Take multiple tissue and fluid samples at washout for culture.
Start physiotherapy once the acute inflammation settles to preserve range of movement.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Daily clinical review of pain, effusion, range of movement and temperature, with serial CRP to track the trend.
Failure to improve suggests inadequate drainage, a resistant organism or another diagnosis: re-aspirate, review cultures, and consider washout.
Monitor vancomycin levels and renal function; adjust cefuroxime, cefazolin and vancomycin doses in renal impairment.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Starting antibiotics before aspiration in a stable patient, leaving the infection culture-negative.
Diagnosing gout because crystals are seen and missing coexisting infection.
Missing gonococcal infection in young adults, or tuberculosis in a chronic monoarthritis.
Undertreating the hip, which rarely drains adequately by needle alone.
Stopping IV antibiotics too early in S. aureus bacteraemia (needs a full bacteraemia work-up).

drugs.name: Flucloxacillin
drugs.notes: First choice without risk factors for atypical organisms.

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.notes: Alternative anti-staphylococcal agent; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Cefuroxime
drugs.notes: Older or frail patients, recurrent urinary infection (gram-negative risk).

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours (30 mg/kg/day), adjusted to levels
drugs.notes: MRSA risk; combine with a 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin; adjust for renal function.
